title: ExpressJS and PokeAPI
summary: A small Express app I built for a course using the PokeAPI.
content:
In a previous course, we had to work with the PokeAPI, but I wanted to go a bit further than the basic requirements. Instead of just fetching data, I focused on making the app more visually appealing and adding extra functionality. The backend uses Express to handle requests to the PokeAPI, and the app can be run locally using Live Server and the server on port 3000. Overall, it was a fun project that helped me better understand working with external APIs and structuring a simple Express app. You can check out the GitHub repo here: 
    [Random Pokémon Generator](https://github.com/RiveraTerryn-FS/randompokemongen)

title: Why Folder Structure Matters More Than I Expected
summary: A short post on how better folder structure has made my projects easier to work with and maintain.
content:
While working on multiple projects this term, one thing that stood out to me was how important folder structure really is. In earlier projects, I tended to put most of my logic into a small number of files just to get things working. While that approach worked at first, it quickly became hard to read and even harder to debug.

As projects grew larger, separating concerns into clearly named folders made a big difference. Breaking things up into areas like components, data, styles, and utilities helped me understand my own code better when coming back to it later. It also made it easier to spot bugs and make changes without accidentally breaking unrelated features.

Another benefit of better structure was reusability. When components and logic are organized cleanly, it becomes much easier to reuse them across different pages or projects. Instead of rewriting similar code, I could move or import existing pieces with confidence.

Overall, improving my folder structure has helped me write cleaner code and spend less time searching through files. It is something I plan to continue working on in future projects.

title: Getting Started with React Native
summary: An overview of React Native and how it is easy to learn if you already know React, including styling and API integration.
content:
![React Native Cover](https://terrynrivera.me/cdn/blog/react-native-cover.png)

If you already understand React basics like components, props, state, and hooks, then React Native feels very familiar and is not hard to pick up.

React Native is a framework created by Facebook (now Meta) that allows developers to build mobile applications using JavaScript and React. Instead of building web apps that run in a browser, you build apps that run on iOS and Android using the same component-based structure.

One of the biggest advantages of React Native is how similar it is to React. You still create functional components, use hooks like useState and useEffect, and structure your project in a similar way. The main difference is that instead of using HTML elements like div, h1, or p, you use built-in components such as View, Text, and ScrollView. This makes the transition from web development to mobile development much easier.

Styling in React Native is also simple. It does not use traditional CSS files. Instead, styles are written in JavaScript using objects. The syntax feels similar to styled-components in React because you are writing styles directly inside your component files. You define styles using StyleSheet.create and apply them to components. It keeps everything organized and easy to manage.

Another thing I like about React Native is how easy it is to connect to an API. You can use fetch or libraries like axios just like you would in a regular React app. The process of making API calls, storing the response in state, and rendering the data to the screen is almost the same as it is on the web.

Overall, React Native is a great option for developers who already know React and want to move into mobile app development.

title: Password Hashing and bcrypt
summary: A short explanation of why password hashing matters and how bcrypt protects user credentials.
content:
![Password-Hashing-Bcrypt/Screenshot](https://terrynrivera.me/cdn/blog/passwordhash-cover.png)

When building an application with user authentication, one of the most important security practices is password hashing. You should never store plain text passwords in your database. If your database is ever leaked, plain text passwords would immediately expose every user's account.

Instead, passwords should be hashed.

---

## What Is Password Hashing?

Hashing converts a password into a scrambled string of characters using a cryptographic algorithm. Unlike encryption, hashing is one way. Once a password is hashed, it cannot be turned back into the original password.

For example, instead of storing:

```
password123
```

You store something like:

```
$2b$10$9uGxK1pF6...
```

Even if someone gains access to the database, they cannot easily determine the original password from that hash.

---

## Why bcrypt?

bcrypt is a popular hashing function designed specifically for passwords. It improves security in two major ways:

- It automatically adds a salt  
- It is intentionally slow  

A salt is a random value added to the password before hashing. This ensures that even if two users have the same password, their hashes will still be different. This helps protect against rainbow table attacks.

bcrypt is also designed to be slow on purpose. That may sound strange, but it makes brute force attacks much harder. If an attacker tries to guess passwords millions of times per second, a slow hashing function significantly limits how fast they can do that.

---

## How It Works in Code

When a user registers:

```js
const hashedPassword = await bcrypt.hash(password, 10);
```

When they log in:

```js
const isMatch = await bcrypt.compare(password, user.password);
```

bcrypt handles the salt and comparison internally, which makes it both secure and easy to use.

---

In short, bcrypt protects user passwords by hashing them securely, adding randomness with salting, and slowing down potential attackers. Any modern web application that stores user credentials should use a secure hashing function like bcrypt instead of saving passwords directly.
